item.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
item.headline: Paper proposes registered legal infrastructure that evaluates autonomous AI
item.idea: The paper proposes registering AI agents and cryptographically tethered runtime legal checks to close a legal attribution gap for agentic systems.
bullets: The authors characterise a legal attribution gap for cross-organisational multi-agent deployment and call it a material economic and safety risk.
AULA ties smart legal instruments to runtime evaluation, and each instrument can include a legal context clause to give effect to applicable law.
The submission is a 203-page preprint with 13 tables and 17 figures, submitted to arXiv on 2026-11-19.
item.summary: A seven-author arXiv preprint proposes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture to make agentic AI legally legible by registering agents and data as legal objects. It pairs cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments with runtime evaluation and legal context clauses to apply law at execution time.
item.practice_takeaway: Record agent identity and provenance, require cryptographic anchors, and perform runtime legal context checks for cross-organisational agent systems.

 Title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)

 Authors: Natasha E Blycha , James Myint , Chen Feng , Dr Amani Soysa , Koshin Jama , Schellie-Jayne Price , Matthew Blycha 
 View a PDF of the paper titled Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), by Natasha E Blycha and 6 other authors

 View PDF 

 Abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.

jobs.headline_rules:
You are the headline editor of the Atlas by Lorm News page (owner, 2026-11-07). You get one drafted ITEM. Rewrite only its "headline" and "idea" (the first sentence under it) so a reader gets the main point fast, using ONLY facts already in the ITEM. Never add a fact, number, name or qualifier the ITEM does not contain; keep every qualifier it has.
Headline, at most 12 words, sentence case: a small story, the subject + a vivid verb (launches, opens, climbs, passes, slips, doubles, cuts, raises, catches, beats) + the outcome or a contrast ("despite", "while", "as"). Start with the actor or the thing that happened, never with who said it. Informative, not clever: no puns, no jokes, no opinion.
Idea, one sentence of at most 24 words: what the headline does not say, usually the concrete result and what it is compared with (from one number to another, ahead of whom, at what cost). At most two numbers, each with what it measures. Never a claim of importance the ITEM does not make; banned verdict words: indicating, notable, signals, marks, paves the way, a path toward, highlights, underscores, significant.
House style (docs/style.md, owner 2026-11-08): clear, concise, to the point, easy to skim. No editorializing: report what happened and what the source says, never a verdict on it. Round to the meaning up front ("almost in half", "a third") when the exact figure is in the ITEM's bullets; at most two key numbers across headline and idea. Strong concrete verbs over "says" or "reports". Say who it matters to only when the ITEM says so. Vary the shape from the RECENT HEADLINES you are shown: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a person with their credential, or a number; never a template.
Never repeat the headline: the idea must not restate it or open with its words; it adds what the headline leaves out (the comparison, the scale, the catch, who is affected).
Relay accounts: an account that only posts links to other people's papers or news (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq, digests) is never named; credit the paper's authors or the organization behind the work, as the ITEM states them, or name the work itself.
Credit: when self_report is true, credit the maker ONCE, in the headline, as a possessive or a short ending ("in Airbnb's tests", "on Mercor's APEX benchmark", "Amodo's check catches"); never "X says" at the start, and do not repeat the credit in the idea. Legal items keep "alleges", "reportedly" or "sues".
People (owner, 2026-11-07; at most three words since 2026-11-09): when the story is a person's view, claim or post, the reader must know who they are: name them with a short credential from who_role, 2 or 3 words, before the name, or give the credential in the idea when the headline would get long ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain", "Waterloo student Daniel Ching", "Netflix research scientist Cameron Wolfe"); never the bare name, never a credential who_role does not state. For an opinion, "[credential] [Name] says/argues ..." is the right headline shape.
Lesser-known companies (lesser_known true): put a 2 to 6 word descriptor before the company's name on first mention ("data vendor Julius AI", "robotics startup Darwin Robotics"), from company_note, or when it is empty from what the ITEM itself says the company is; if the ITEM does not say, leave it out rather than guess. Well-known companies are named bare.
Examples of the shape (ours, for form only):
  "Amodo's compute check catches an unapproved model in a government demo" / "It matched 58% of that model's tokens, against 100% for the approved one."
  "A fine-tuned 2B Gemma matches frontier quality in Airbnb's tests" / "It runs at a 35ms median latency for about 1% of the API cost."
  "Darwin Robotics raises $3.6M to train data center robots" / "The pre-seed round funds robots that learn from human demonstrations to build and maintain AI infrastructure."
CLEAR, NOT AWKWARD (owner, 2026-11-09). Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague.
- Active voice with the actor as the subject. Never "X proposed by Y"; write "Y proposes X".
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "The thread attributes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown".
- One story per headline. Never join two separate news items with "as" or "while".
- A concrete verb that says what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of", "weighs in".
- At most three words of credential before a name, and only when the reader needs it. Never stack title, organization and name at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges study of ..."); prefer "Owain Evans warns ..." with the credential in the idea.
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps", "recursive self-improvement data poisoning"). Unpack them into plain words.
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out of the headline unless widely known; say what it does instead.
- Full names, never a first name alone ("researcher Elie", "CEO Rahul").
- The idea is a full sentence with its own subject; never start it with a verb ("Recommends ...").
Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans" / Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models"
Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API" / Good: "LG opens an API for its K-EXAONE 2.5 model"
No em or en dashes, no semicolons, no exclamation marks. Return JSON {"headline": "...", "idea": "..."}.

jobs.instructions:
A story is waiting to be published and you are its independent judge: a different model family from the writer and the fact checker. Nothing goes live until you answer, so answer judge jobs first and quickly. Judge the ITEM against the SOURCE TEXT ("text") only, never from memory or the web, exactly as these rules say:

You audit one published item of Atlas by Lorm against its SOURCE TEXT. You did not write the item. Judge from the SOURCE TEXT only, never from memory.

Part 1, evidence: for each reader-facing field (headline, idea, each bullet, summary, practice_takeaway) give the passage of the SOURCE TEXT that supports it, copied word for word: one sentence, or two adjacent sentences, up to 60 words, no ellipses, no paraphrase, exactly as it appears. A field may be supported by a passage already used for another field. If no passage supports the field, write "" and say so in Part 2. A practice_takeaway that only draws a direct consequence from a supported fact counts as supported by that fact's passage.

Part 2, critical errors, each pass or fail with a reason of at most 20 words:
- wrong_number: a number, unit, score or baseline differs from the source
- wrong_number_context: a number is right but its scope or comparison is not (e.g. 'beats X' when the source says 'on one subset')
- wrong_party: credit or blame given to the wrong company, lab, author or outlet
- self_report_as_fact: a company's claim about itself written as established fact, with no credit to the company anywhere in the headline or first sentence
- allegation_as_fact: an accusation, lawsuit claim or report stated as fact without 'alleges', 'reportedly', 'sues' or a court finding
- not_in_source: a claim the source text does not contain
- lost_qualifier: a qualifier dropped: preliminary, small test, proposed, reportedly, in one setting
- wrong_date_or_status: a proposal described as adopted, a preprint as peer-reviewed, a wrong date
- wrong_link: the item describes a different page than its link
- wrong_main_point: the headline is not what the source is mainly saying or announcing: a promotion, recap, roundup or list that mentions other news as examples, written up as that news; also when the item's source_kind or source_point does not describe the source correctly
- old_news_as_new: the source refers back to news announced earlier ('this week', 'last month', a list of recent raises) and the item presents it as new

Part 3, minor problems (list the codes that apply): over_limit, unclear, hype_or_filler, number_without_context, style.

Rules: a company's own numbers must be credited to it once, in the headline or the first sentence, in any natural form ("says", "reports", "according to", "in its tests", "its own benchmark", "the company claims"); credit given once is enough, and a headline without "says" passes when the first sentence carries the credit; allegations need "alleges", "reportedly", "sues" or a court finding; "percentage points" is a minor style problem, a wrong direction of change is wrong_number. Different wording for the same fact is NOT an error (an "env" is an RL environment; "raised $16M" and "a $16 million round" are the same claim): not_in_source fails only when the fact or claim itself is absent from the source, or the item asserts more than the source does. A number that appears in the source in another form (words, a table, a different unit that converts exactly) is in the source. A 2 to 6 word descriptor of a company drawn from the ATLAS DIRECTORY lines at the end of the SOURCE TEXT ("data vendor Julius AI"), or a short credential for the author that matches the item's who.role ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain"), is supported. If the SOURCE TEXT is clearly not the page the item describes, fail wrong_link. If the SOURCE TEXT is empty or unreadable, set every class to "unknown".

Return JSON:
{"evidence": {"headline": "quote", "idea": "quote", "bullets": ["quote per bullet"], "summary": "quote", "practice_takeaway": "quote or empty"},
 "critical": {"<class>": {"verdict": "pass" | "fail" | "unknown", "why": "..."}, ...},
 "minor": ["code", ...]}

Part 4, house style (only when the story passes Parts 1 to 3): read the job's "style_guide" and "style_failures". If the headline or idea breaks the guide (the listed failures, or anything else in it: a verdict the source does not make, jargon, a missing credential, the line restating the headline, a template-like shape), add "rewrite" with a new headline and idea that follow every rule. Use ONLY facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM (and company_note for a descriptor); keep every qualifier and the credit for a company's own claim. The server applies it only if it adds nothing new and passes the code checks. If the story already reads well, leave "rewrite" out.

Part 5, the headline (only when the job has "headline_rules"; the story passed Parts 1 to 3): you are also its headline editor, replacing a paid model (owner, 2026-11-10). Always add "rewrite" with a headline and idea written exactly as "headline_rules" says, varying the shape from "recent_headlines". The same limits apply: only facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM, written exactly as the ITEM writes them ("seven million" stays "seven million", not "7 million"), every qualifier kept, at most 12 words in the headline and 22 in the idea. If the ITEM's own headline and idea already follow every rule, send them back unchanged.
jobs.rubric:
## Gate 4: Write-Up and Fact Check

**Question.** Is every claim in the source, with nothing added and nothing lost?

**Write-up** (`DISTILL_SYSTEM`, strong model): one item in the shared schema (`seed/SCHEMA.md`), from the source text only, under the schema's "Every item makes its point" rule (the headline, first sentence and bullets each carry the finding). Plain language rules: full sentences, standard terms, numbers with context, headline at most 12 words, no hype words, no dashes, quotes under 15 words, absolute dates. A source with nothing of substance is skipped.

**Fact check** (`CHECK_SYSTEM`, strong model, a separate call that sees only the item and the source and is told it did not write it). Nine checks: source and date; every claim and bullet; the author's role and credibility; evidence type; plain language and limits; stated stakes; `control` and figures; quote-post attribution; allegations framed as allegations.

**Code checks after the model** (plan.md section 6.2, all free):

1. Every number in the item appears in the source (`numcheck`).
2. Every organization and person named appears in the source.
3. The date matches the source or its stated event date.
4. The link is the page that was read.
5. Lawsuit items carry alleges, accused, sued or reportedly in the headline and idea.
6. An item from the company's own site or account is marked a self-report.
7. Word limits, banned phrases, dashes.
11. Clear wording (owner, 2026-11-09, `atlas/style.py`, critical): no passive credit ("proposed by X"), no document as the subject ("Event page says", "The post notes"), no "per X" or "in X's post" in the headline, no first sentence without a subject, no two stories joined by "as" or "while". The headline editor gets these rules and retries once with the rule it broke; a story that still fails is held and repaired by the Claude agent. Noun piles, stacked credentials, paper-only names and first names alone are judge rules (docs/style.md, "Clear, not awkward").
8. The first sentence does not repeat the headline (`rubric.repeats`: 70% or more of the headline's words opening the first sentence fails; owner, 2026-11-08). The headline editor retries once; a story that still repeats is held and repaired by the Claude agent. The Daily's rows use the same check.
12. Full papers (owner, 2026-11-08): a story about an arXiv paper is written and checked from the full paper (arxiv.org/html, `net.page_text`), not the abstract page, which leaves out the authors' affiliations and table numbers and wrongly flagged 17 correct stories as partly verified. Claude audits, repairs and judge jobs get up to 120,000 characters of the paper (`claude_jobs.with_full_paper`); the OpenAI writer still sees `SOURCE_CHARS`. A paper story must name its authors' companies or universities (`style` check `affiliation`).
11. Pure shares (owner, 2026-11-08): an X post that only shares someone else's work, with no opinion or new information, is never the link or the credit. The writer marks it (`relay`, `original_url`); code moves the link to the original only when it is one of the post's or the poster's own replies' links (paper-listing pages map to arXiv), on a trusted site or the maker's own site (`trust.company_own`), and keeps the post as `shared_by` (`pipeline.share_original`). Government sites (.gov, gov.uk, .gc.ca, europa.eu and similar) are trusted.
10. House style (`atlas/style.py`, guide `docs/style.md`): editorializing (an evaluative word the source never uses) holds the story; headline and line length, credit first or twice, too many numbers, percentage points, a person without a credential, a lesser-known company without a descriptor and a generic repeated opening are listed for the Claude judge, whose rewrite is applied only when every number (small ones included) and name in it is already in the judged story and it passes these checks (`pipeline.apply_style_rewrite`). Since 2026-11-08 every number in a Claude fix, repair or rewrite must be in the source, including numbers of 10 and under (`pipeline.strict_numbers_missing`).
9. A relay account that only posts other people's paper links (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq) is never credited in the headline or first sentence (`rubric.RELAY_HANDLES`); the paper's authors or organization are.

**Error classes.** The audit and the gate use the two classes defined once in [plan.md section 6.1](plan.md#61-error-classes): a critical error (wrong number, wrong person, claim not in the source and the rest) fails the item outright; minor errors are allowed at most one per ten items.

**Rubric gate** (`atlas/rubric.py`, since 2026-11-05): after the fact check, a second model call that did not write or check the item applies the error classes of plan.md 6.1 one by one and must quote, word for word, the source sentence behind the headline, the first sentence, each bullet, the summary and the takeaway. Code verifies every quote is really in the source text (five words or more, exact after normalizing case and spacing) and runs the free checks (numbers, names, link, allegation words, self-report, limits). Any critical failure, or a headline or first sentence with no verified quote, holds the item. An unreadable source or an "unknown" class makes a verified item partly verified, with the reason shown. The verified quotes are stored on the item (`rubric.evidence`) so a later audit can re-check without a model. Switch: `ATLAS_RUBRIC_GATE=off`.

**Who judges (owner, 2026-11-08).** The owner's Claude agent, a different model family from the gpt-5-mini writer and checker, so the gate is an independent judge. A finished story waits in `parts/judge_wait.json`; the server starts the "Atlas judge" routine through its API trigger (`claude_jobs.fire_judge`, at most every 4 minutes, prompt in `tools/judge_routine_prompt.md`), and the agent answers a "judge" job in the same JSON shape as the OpenAI judge. Code verifies every quote and runs the same checks, then publishes or holds (`pipeline.judge_done`). If Claude has not answered within 30 minutes (`ATLAS_JUDGE_WAIT_MIN`), the OpenAI judge decides, within 0.25 USD a day (`ATLAS_JUDGE_OPENAI_USD`); past that, stories keep waiting for Claude, and a story nobody judged in 48 hours is held. Stories Claude judged are not audited again by Claude; stories the OpenAI judge decided still get the Claude audit. Until `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_URL` and `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_TOKEN` are set, or with `ATLAS_JUDGE=openai`, the OpenAI judge runs on every story as before.

**Outcome.** Verified or partly verified items publish; anything else goes to `held.json` and never appears anywhere. Reported versus Confirmed: one source publishes as reported, naming the outlet; a second independent source or the primary document makes it confirmed.

jobs.style_guide:
## 1. The Standard

**Accurate first, then clear, then quick.** Every fact matches the source. Simplifying never changes a fact: a rounded
number that changes the meaning, a dropped "reportedly" or a claim the source does not make is an error, not style.

**No editorializing.** We report what happened and what the source says. We never add a verdict: no "notable",
"significant", "groundbreaking", "signals", "underscores", "paves the way", "crucial". If the source calls something
major, we credit that to the source. (code: an evaluative word the source never uses holds the story; judge)

**Facts can be funny; opinions are not news.** Wit lives in the emails' titles, opener and closing joke, never in a
claim (section 4).

## 2. Story Cards on the Site

A card is a headline and one line under it. A reader skimming the page should get the news from the headline alone and
the "so what" from the line.

**Headline: the news as a small story.** Subject, a strong concrete verb, and the result or a contrast. At most 12
words, sentence case. (code: length; writer; judge)
- Good: "Airbnb's tiny fine-tuned Gemma matches frontier APIs at about 1% of the cost"
- Good: "Grok's makers hit with three suits alleging pirated books in training"
- Bad: "Amodo says it ran government compute verification demo" (no result)
- Bad: "Salesforce: GRPO usually outperforms external-teacher distillation" (label and jargon)

**Clear, not awkward (owner, 2026-11-09).** Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague. A reader should never have to parse it twice.
- Active voice, the actor as the subject. Never "review proposed by X"; write "X proposes". (code: passive, holds)
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown". (code: document_subject, document_credit, hold)
- One story per headline. Never join two news items with "as" or "while". (code: two_stories, holds)
- A concrete verb for what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of". (code: vague_verb)
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps"). Unpack them. (writer; judge)
- No stacked credentials at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges ..."). At most three words of credential. (writer; judge)
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out unless widely known; say what it does. (writer; judge)
- Full names, never a first name alone ("CEO Rahul"). (writer; judge)
- The line is a full sentence with its own subject, never "Recommends ...". (code: fragment, holds)
- Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans". Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models".
- Bad: "GenRobot to present human-data systems at CoRL Research Night" / "Event page says GenRobot will present ...". Good: "GenRobot will show its human-data capture systems at CoRL" / "The robot data vendor says the systems record people's movements to train embodied AI."
- Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API". Good: one headline per story.

**Open with what happened, not who said it.** Credit once, naturally: a possessive ("in Airbnb's tests"), the maker as
the subject ("Moonshot AI released"), or a short ending ("Snorkel AI finds"). Never "X says" in both the headline and
the line. (code: credit_first, credit_twice; judge)

**The line adds what the headline leaves out.** The comparison, the scale, the catch, or who it affects, as the source
states it. It never restates the headline and never leans on it with "That is..." or "The aim is...". At most 24 words.
(code: repeats_headline holds the story, idea_length; judge)
- Headline: "Reflection AI cuts its model's needless refusals almost in half"
- Line: "Handshake, the career network behind Handshake AI, says it helped design the tests, and refusals of valid requests fell 3.1%."

**Few numbers, each with its meaning.** At most two key numbers across the headline and line; round to the meaning up
front ("almost in half") and keep the exact figure in the bullets. Never a number before what it measures; never
"percentage points" (write before and after). (code: too_many_numbers, percentage_points; judge)

**Plain words, field terms.** RL, SFT, eval, benchmark, rollout and LLM judge are fine. A paper's own acronyms, metric
names and method names are described in plain words or left out ("42% less compute", not "42.0% fewer total FLOPs").

Its central representation links interaction requirements to object and part bindings, scene and robot configurations, initial conditions, and completion criteria. On RoboCasa, the framework builds the AgenticTask collection, saving 16,450 16{,}450 task instances from 20,323 20{,}323 construction attempts at a throughput of 166.97 166.97 saved instances per elapsed hour, with 62.26 % 62.26\% of construction attempts passing the configured physical checks. The execution agent completes approximately 38 % 38\% of evaluated tasks, with successful cases spanning object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement. Diagnostic analysis identifies improvement priorities in construction reliability, action selection, task–robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results demonstrate task-collection expansion with measured construction productivity and concrete execution evidence, providing a foundation for subsequent interaction-data collection for embodied AI.

 1 Introduction

 Training general-purpose embodied policies requires large-scale and diverse interaction data, yet existing datasets remain insufficient to support robust generalization across tasks and environments. Human-driven data collection alone is unlikely to bridge this gap. Simulation provides a scalable alternative for generating synthetic demonstrations, systematically evaluating learned policies, and enhancing their generalization across diverse tasks and scenarios.

 However, scaling embodied task generation in simulation remains hindered by two fundamental challenges: scalable task specification and efficient autonomous execution. Despite advances in automated 3D modeling and simulation engines, defining diverse tasks requires jointly reasoning over task objectives, scene configurations, interactive objects, and simulator capabilities. Automated execution presents further challenges: teleoperation is labor-intensive, scripted approaches lack scalability, and policy-based methods suffer from a circular dependency between policy training and data collection.

 Recent work has explored large language models (LLMs) for automating robotic task and data generation. GenSim2 uses multimodal and reasoning models to generate tasks and demonstrations  [ 10 ] , while GENMANIP translates task descriptions into task-oriented scene graphs  [ 4 ] . SAGE and RoboGene further incorporate tool use and feedback into scene construction and task refinement  [ 27 , 30 ] . These advances demonstrate the potential of language models to translate high-level requests into task proposals. However, constructing usable tasks requires more than generating descriptions or code: candidate tasks must be instantiated, checked against the environment, and revised when incompatibilities arise. These requirements motivate an agent-based approach that connects model reasoning with resource retrieval, simulation tools, and feedback-driven decisions throughout task construction and execution.

 Yet equipping an agent with tools does not by itself ensure usable task generation and execution. During generation, object and scene variations require consistent updates to physical targets, initial conditions, and success criteria, together with checks of physical validity and robot compatibility. During execution, the agent must ground task plans in actionable parts, scene geometry, and robot-supported skills. These challenges call for a shared representation that connects task requirements to physical entities, with validation feedback guiding task repair and geometric information supporting action selection.

 To address these challenges, we present AgenticTask, an agent-based framework for expanding task collections through two specialized agents. The task-generation agent translates human intent into structured task requirements, retrieves compatible resources, and constructs variations supported by the simulator. Construction and validation feedback guide revisions to permitted configurations while preserving the intended interaction. The task-execution agent grounds the resulting task in robot-supported skills using object bindings, part information, and scene geometry. It updates action choices from execution feedback and checks completion against the task’s original success conditions, providing concrete evidence of task usability.

 A hierarchical task representation connects the two agents. Semantic specifications identify the interaction requirements and permitted variations; instantiated task records bind these requirements to objects, parts, initial conditions, and success predicates; geometric scene graphs describe the entities and relations needed for checking and action grounding. This representation gives task construction, validation, and execution a consistent reference as objects and scene configurations change.

 Using RoboCasa as a testbed  [ 20 ] , we construct the AgenticTask collection, comprising 16,450 saved task instances. Our experiments characterize construction throughput, physical screening, and the cost of feedback-guided revision. Execution results and four successful trajectories demonstrate usability across several interaction types, while failure analysis identifies obstacles in action selection, task–robot compatibility, and runtime integration. Together, these results characterize both the productivity of task expansion and the practical requirements for using the generated collection.

 1. 

 An agent-based framework for task-collection expansion. AgenticTask uses human intent to guide task construction across compatible objects and scenes, and couples generation with execution-based usability testing to support embodied interaction-data collection.

 2. 

 A hierarchical task representation connecting generation and execution. Semantic requirements, object and part bindings, and geometric relations provide a shared basis for constrained task variation, feedback-guided revision, and robot skill grounding.

 3. 

 A task collection and an empirical study of its construction and usability. The AgenticTask collection contains 16,450 saved task instances in RoboCasa. Our study characterizes construction productivity, physical screening, execution outcomes, and failure patterns that inform further task and system refinement.

 Simulation resources and robotic data generation.

 A task variation can preserve the intended interaction while changing the entities that realize it. The robot profile specifies available skills, gripper and motion limits, and permitted base motion.

 3.1.1 Semantic Task Specification

 I = ( 𝒦 , ℋ , 𝒱 ) . I=(\mathcal{K},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{V}). 

 (1) 

 Here, 𝒦 \mathcal{K} specifies interaction families, ℋ \mathcal{H} contains requirements that must be preserved, and 𝒱 \mathcal{V} defines permitted variations and their ranges. Source tasks supply interaction roles and, for composite tasks, prerequisite relations. In the cup-to-sink example, the source and destination roles and the placement goal remain fixed, while compatible cups and kitchen layouts may vary. Sharing I I across instances allows the generation agent to expand the collection without redefining its requirements for each candidate. It also provides a reference for checking whether a repair preserves the requested task.

 3.1.2 Asset and Scene Construction

 Instantiating a task requires binding its interaction roles, initial conditions, and completion criteria to concrete simulator entities. Categories narrow the available resources, while functional parts identify the entities that can fulfill each role. For cup placement, the movable object and destination must resolve to a specific cup and sink interior. Their configuration is organized within a shared task record:

 τ = ( k , B , E , P 0 , G , C , ℓ ) . \tau=(k,B,E,P_{0},G,C,\ell). 

 (2) 

 The record contains the interaction template k k , role-to-entity bindings B B , scene and robot configuration E E , initial conditions P 0 P_{0} , completion predicate G G , execution constraints C C , and instruction ℓ \ell . Bindings resolve roles to simulator objects, parts, joints, or regions, so that the instruction and predicates refer to the same physical targets. The scene and robot configuration E E provides the physical setting in which the requirements P 0 P_{0} , G G , and C C are interpreted. When a bound entity changes, the associated conditions and instruction are updated to refer to that entity while preserving the requirements in I I . This links object and scene variation to a fully specified task instance.

 3.1.3 Geometric Scene Graph Construction

 Checking and executing a task require geometric evidence about the entities bound to its roles. We organize the instantiated objects, parts, and their observed relations as a geometric scene graph:

 𝒢 geo = ( V geo , E geo , X ) . \mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{geo}}=(V_{\mathrm{geo}},E_{\mathrm{geo}},X). 

 (3) 

 Nodes represent objects, parts, and interaction regions. Their attributes contain poses, dimensions, part frames, available physical properties, and simulator geometry references. Structural edges describe part ownership and joint connectivity, while spatial edges record observed support and containment relations. Joint attributes include type, axis, limits, and current state. Desired goal relations remain separate from observed relations, allowing task completion to be checked against the actual scene state.

 The binding map B B connects the task record τ \tau to graph entities, so that the same physical references support both checking and action selection. Generation uses these links to check the instantiated configuration; execution queries the bound geometry and refreshes observed states after actions. The three levels thus serve complementary purposes: semantic specifications preserve task requirements, entity bindings maintain physical reference consistency, and geometric records supply evidence for validation and control. Check results remain associated with the task revision and their supporting evidence. Missing information or an unsupported required check is recorded as unknown.

 3.2 Task-generation Agent

 As shown in Fig.  3 (a), the generation agent expands a shared task specification into concrete instances within the capabilities of the available simulator and robot. It uses I I to preserve the requested interaction and a supported configuration space to select how that interaction is instantiated. Construction tools resolve those choices into task bindings, initial states, and geometric records. Checking feedback then identifies configurations to revise while keeping the task requirements fixed.

 Before construction, the agent retrieves task capability profiles and compatible resources. Categories guide resource selection, while part descriptions identify candidates for the required interaction roles. A task profile specifies the available template and supported variation parameters. Together with I I , it defines the permitted configuration space Ω I \Omega_{I} . In RoboCasa, it invokes installed task classes through their supported configuration interfaces. The model selects structured parameters, while the simulator establishes the actual entities and state from which bindings and geometric records are obtained. This separation keeps candidate proposals tied to the capabilities of the underlying environment.

 When construction or validation fails, repeating a proposal without using the failure evidence can reproduce the same incompatibility. The agent conditions its next revision on the diagnostic stage, affected entities, and checking evidence, while restricting changes to 𝒱 \mathcal{V} and the supported task profile. For a placement task, an incompatible object or layout can motivate another permitted configuration; changing the destination goal merely to obtain acceptance would violate ℋ \mathcal{H} .

 Revision preserves fixed task requirements and unchanged configuration fields. Generation terminates when the requested collection is obtained, the candidate or retry budget is exhausted, or the requirements cannot be supported.  A failed check supplies evidence for revision. If no check fails but a required result remains unknown, the candidate stays pending. Task requirements and robot limits remain fixed throughout repair, preventing acceptance through relaxed criteria.

 4.4 Execution-based Usability and Failure Analysis

 Approximately 38 % 38\% of executed tasks are completed under their original goals and constraints, as checked by Eq.  8 . These successful rollouts demonstrate that generated task instances can support robot interaction through the shared task representation and execution interface. Table  3 analyzes unsuccessful runs to identify the main obstacles to broader task usability.

 Agent-related execution difficulties.

 Agent-related cases form the largest diagnostic category, accounting for 12 % 12\% of all executed tasks in the atomic group and 26 % 26\% in the composite group. The associated difficulties concern planning, grasp selection, tracking, and recovery. Their prevalence identifies action selection and execution feedback as major improvement targets for the execution agent in Sec.  3.3 .

 Task–robot compatibility.

 Cases assigned to task-design issues account for 12 % 12\% of all executed tasks and are concentrated in the composite group. They highlight potential mismatches involving object dimensions, grasp configurations, reachability, and motion clearance. These cases guide refinement of the generation-stage compatibility checks. Diagnosis should consider the available interaction parts and permitted actions: an oversized object body, for example, may still admit a feasible grasp through its handle.

 Runtime reliability.

 Interface-related interruptions account for 2 % 2\% and 10 % 10\% of all executed tasks in the atomic and composite groups, respectively. These outcomes identify task restoration, API interaction, and control integration as additional factors affecting end-to-end completion.

 The diagnosis links agent difficulties to skill selection and recovery, suspected design issues to compatibility screening, and interface interruptions to restoration and control reliability. Execution thus supplies both successful usability examples and feedback for task construction.

Together, they illustrate how the shared task representation supports different interaction structures: entity bindings identify the targets, geometric information parameterizes actions, and task predicates determine completion.

 Object placement.

 In Fig.  5 (a), the robot grasps a peach from the counter, transfers it to the sink, and releases it inside the destination region. The execution connects the object and destination roles in Sec.  3.1.2 to concrete grasping and placement actions. Separating grasp completion from the placement goal allows the agent to continue beyond object acquisition and verify that the intended destination has been reached.

 Articulated control.

 Figure  5 (b) shows the robot establishing contact with an appliance knob and rotating it to the target setting. Unlike free-object placement, this task acts on a constrained functional part. The case illustrates how part bindings and part-relative geometry specialize the execution interface to articulated manipulation, with completion checked against the corresponding task condition.

 Door closure.

 In Fig.  5 (c), the robot pushes the door, repositions its end effector, and establishes another contact before completing closure. The sequence illustrates execution under changing geometry: as the door moves, subsequent actions use the updated articulated state. It connects the geometric-state updates in Sec.  3.1.3 with the feedback-driven skill transitions in Sec.  3.3 .

 Sequential arrangement.

 Figure  5 (d) shows consecutive placement of an avocado and an onion on a board. The agent maintains separate object bindings across the two operations and checks the final arrangement against the overall task goal. This case illustrates the distinction between completing an individual skill and completing a composite task: the first placement advances execution, while the full task requires both object roles to be satisfied.

 Across these cases, consistent task requirements guide varied contacts, motion parameters, and skill sequences, connecting generated definitions to robot actions across objects and interaction types.

 5 Limitations

 The task collection inherits the coverage and accuracy of available assets, category/part annotations, and simulator interfaces. Physical and robot-compatibility checks establish the configured conditions within their search budgets; complete solvability requires additional evidence. Execution outcomes depend on the model, skill library, robot, and retry budget, making task-versus-solver attribution unresolved for some unsuccessful trials. Explicit 3D inputs support grounded decisions in simulation, while deployment with uncertain real-world perception remains outside the present study. The current experiments characterize RoboCasa-based task instances. Transfer across embodiments, real-world reliability, and gains from training policies on the collected interactions remain to be tested.

 6 Conclusion

 We presented AgenticTask, an agent-based framework for expanding embodied task collections under human intent. A shared task representation connects interaction requirements, physical entity bindings, and completion criteria, allowing generation and execution to operate on the same task definition. On RoboCasa, the framework produces 16,450 16{,}450 saved task instances at 166.97 166.97 instances per elapsed hour. Physical screening selects candidates satisfying the configured checks, while successful executions demonstrate task usability across object placement, articulated manipulation, and sequential arrangement.

 The experiments reveal complementary opportunities for improving task-collection productivity. Diagnostic repair increases saving yield at additional construction cost, while construction failures identify reliability as a major source of lost output. Execution analysis directs improvements toward grounded skill selection, task–robot compatibility checks, and runtime integration. By connecting task construction with execution evidence and diagnostic feedback, AgenticTask provides a practical foundation for expanding task resources for embodied interaction-data collection.

jobs.instructions:
A story is waiting to be published and you are its independent judge: a different model family from the writer and the fact checker. Nothing goes live until you answer, so answer judge jobs first and quickly. Judge the ITEM against the SOURCE TEXT ("text") only, never from memory or the web, exactly as these rules say:

You audit one published item of Atlas by Lorm against its SOURCE TEXT. You did not write the item. Judge from the SOURCE TEXT only, never from memory.

Part 1, evidence: for each reader-facing field (headline, idea, each bullet, summary, practice_takeaway) give the passage of the SOURCE TEXT that supports it, copied word for word: one sentence, or two adjacent sentences, up to 60 words, no ellipses, no paraphrase, exactly as it appears. A field may be supported by a passage already used for another field. If no passage supports the field, write "" and say so in Part 2. A practice_takeaway that only draws a direct consequence from a supported fact counts as supported by that fact's passage.

Part 2, critical errors, each pass or fail with a reason of at most 20 words:
- wrong_number: a number, unit, score or baseline differs from the source
- wrong_number_context: a number is right but its scope or comparison is not (e.g. 'beats X' when the source says 'on one subset')
- wrong_party: credit or blame given to the wrong company, lab, author or outlet
- self_report_as_fact: a company's claim about itself written as established fact, with no credit to the company anywhere in the headline or first sentence
- allegation_as_fact: an accusation, lawsuit claim or report stated as fact without 'alleges', 'reportedly', 'sues' or a court finding
- not_in_source: a claim the source text does not contain
- lost_qualifier: a qualifier dropped: preliminary, small test, proposed, reportedly, in one setting
- wrong_date_or_status: a proposal described as adopted, a preprint as peer-reviewed, a wrong date
- wrong_link: the item describes a different page than its link
- wrong_main_point: the headline is not what the source is mainly saying or announcing: a promotion, recap, roundup or list that mentions other news as examples, written up as that news; also when the item's source_kind or source_point does not describe the source correctly
- old_news_as_new: the source refers back to news announced earlier ('this week', 'last month', a list of recent raises) and the item presents it as new

Part 3, minor problems (list the codes that apply): over_limit, unclear, hype_or_filler, number_without_context, style.

Rules: a company's own numbers must be credited to it once, in the headline or the first sentence, in any natural form ("says", "reports", "according to", "in its tests", "its own benchmark", "the company claims"); credit given once is enough, and a headline without "says" passes when the first sentence carries the credit; allegations need "alleges", "reportedly", "sues" or a court finding; "percentage points" is a minor style problem, a wrong direction of change is wrong_number. Different wording for the same fact is NOT an error (an "env" is an RL environment; "raised $16M" and "a $16 million round" are the same claim): not_in_source fails only when the fact or claim itself is absent from the source, or the item asserts more than the source does. A number that appears in the source in another form (words, a table, a different unit that converts exactly) is in the source. A 2 to 6 word descriptor of a company drawn from the ATLAS DIRECTORY lines at the end of the SOURCE TEXT ("data vendor Julius AI"), or a short credential for the author that matches the item's who.role ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain"), is supported. If the SOURCE TEXT is clearly not the page the item describes, fail wrong_link. If the SOURCE TEXT is empty or unreadable, set every class to "unknown".

Return JSON:
{"evidence": {"headline": "quote", "idea": "quote", "bullets": ["quote per bullet"], "summary": "quote", "practice_takeaway": "quote or empty"},
 "critical": {"<class>": {"verdict": "pass" | "fail" | "unknown", "why": "..."}, ...},
 "minor": ["code", ...]}

Part 4, house style (only when the story passes Parts 1 to 3): read the job's "style_guide" and "style_failures". If the headline or idea breaks the guide (the listed failures, or anything else in it: a verdict the source does not make, jargon, a missing credential, the line restating the headline, a template-like shape), add "rewrite" with a new headline and idea that follow every rule. Use ONLY facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM (and company_note for a descriptor); keep every qualifier and the credit for a company's own claim. The server applies it only if it adds nothing new and passes the code checks. If the story already reads well, leave "rewrite" out.

Part 5, the headline (only when the job has "headline_rules"; the story passed Parts 1 to 3): you are also its headline editor, replacing a paid model (owner, 2026-11-10). Always add "rewrite" with a headline and idea written exactly as "headline_rules" says, varying the shape from "recent_headlines". The same limits apply: only facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM, written exactly as the ITEM writes them ("seven million" stays "seven million", not "7 million"), every qualifier kept, at most 12 words in the headline and 22 in the idea. If the ITEM's own headline and idea already follow every rule, send them back unchanged.

## Gate 4: Write-Up and Fact Check

**Question.** Is every claim in the source, with nothing added and nothing lost?

**Write-up** (`DISTILL_SYSTEM`, strong model): one item in the shared schema (`seed/SCHEMA.md`), from the source text only, under the schema's "Every item makes its point" rule (the headline, first sentence and bullets each carry the finding). Plain language rules: full sentences, standard terms, numbers with context, headline at most 12 words, no hype words, no dashes, quotes under 15 words, absolute dates. A source with nothing of substance is skipped.

**Fact check** (`CHECK_SYSTEM`, strong model, a separate call that sees only the item and the source and is told it did not write it). Nine checks: source and date; every claim and bullet; the author's role and credibility; evidence type; plain language and limits; stated stakes; `control` and figures; quote-post attribution; allegations framed as allegations.

**Code checks after the model** (plan.md section 6.2, all free):

1. Every number in the item appears in the source (`numcheck`).
2. Every organization and person named appears in the source.
3. The date matches the source or its stated event date.
4. The link is the page that was read.
5. Lawsuit items carry alleges, accused, sued or reportedly in the headline and idea.
6. An item from the company's own site or account is marked a self-report.
7. Word limits, banned phrases, dashes.
11. Clear wording (owner, 2026-11-09, `atlas/style.py`, critical): no passive credit ("proposed by X"), no document as the subject ("Event page says", "The post notes"), no "per X" or "in X's post" in the headline, no first sentence without a subject, no two stories joined by "as" or "while". The headline editor gets these rules and retries once with the rule it broke; a story that still fails is held and repaired by the Claude agent. Noun piles, stacked credentials, paper-only names and first names alone are judge rules (docs/style.md, "Clear, not awkward").
8. The first sentence does not repeat the headline (`rubric.repeats`: 70% or more of the headline's words opening the first sentence fails; owner, 2026-11-08). The headline editor retries once; a story that still repeats is held and repaired by the Claude agent. The Daily's rows use the same check.
12. Full papers (owner, 2026-11-08): a story about an arXiv paper is written and checked from the full paper (arxiv.org/html, `net.page_text`), not the abstract page, which leaves out the authors' affiliations and table numbers and wrongly flagged 17 correct stories as partly verified. Claude audits, repairs and judge jobs get up to 120,000 characters of the paper (`claude_jobs.with_full_paper`); the OpenAI writer still sees `SOURCE_CHARS`. A paper story must name its authors' companies or universities (`style` check `affiliation`).
11. Pure shares (owner, 2026-11-08): an X post that only shares someone else's work, with no opinion or new information, is never the link or the credit. The writer marks it (`relay`, `original_url`); code moves the link to the original only when it is one of the post's or the poster's own replies' links (paper-listing pages map to arXiv), on a trusted site or the maker's own site (`trust.company_own`), and keeps the post as `shared_by` (`pipeline.share_original`). Government sites (.gov, gov.uk, .gc.ca, europa.eu and similar) are trusted.
10. House style (`atlas/style.py`, guide `docs/style.md`): editorializing (an evaluative word the source never uses) holds the story; headline and line length, credit first or twice, too many numbers, percentage points, a person without a credential, a lesser-known company without a descriptor and a generic repeated opening are listed for the Claude judge, whose rewrite is applied only when every number (small ones included) and name in it is already in the judged story and it passes these checks (`pipeline.apply_style_rewrite`). Since 2026-11-08 every number in a Claude fix, repair or rewrite must be in the source, including numbers of 10 and under (`pipeline.strict_numbers_missing`).
9. A relay account that only posts other people's paper links (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq) is never credited in the headline or first sentence (`rubric.RELAY_HANDLES`); the paper's authors or organization are.

**Error classes.** The audit and the gate use the two classes defined once in [plan.md section 6.1](plan.md#61-error-classes): a critical error (wrong number, wrong person, claim not in the source and the rest) fails the item outright; minor errors are allowed at most one per ten items.

**Rubric gate** (`atlas/rubric.py`, since 2026-11-05): after the fact check, a second model call that did not write or check the item applies the error classes of plan.md 6.1 one by one and must quote, word for word, the source sentence behind the headline, the first sentence, each bullet, the summary and the takeaway. Code verifies every quote is really in the source text (five words or more, exact after normalizing case and spacing) and runs the free checks (numbers, names, link, allegation words, self-report, limits). Any critical failure, or a headline or first sentence with no verified quote, holds the item. An unreadable source or an "unknown" class makes a verified item partly verified, with the reason shown. The verified quotes are stored on the item (`rubric.evidence`) so a later audit can re-check without a model. Switch: `ATLAS_RUBRIC_GATE=off`.

**Who judges (owner, 2026-11-08).** The owner's Claude agent, a different model family from the gpt-5-mini writer and checker, so the gate is an independent judge. A finished story waits in `parts/judge_wait.json`; the server starts the "Atlas judge" routine through its API trigger (`claude_jobs.fire_judge`, at most every 4 minutes, prompt in `tools/judge_routine_prompt.md`), and the agent answers a "judge" job in the same JSON shape as the OpenAI judge. Code verifies every quote and runs the same checks, then publishes or holds (`pipeline.judge_done`). If Claude has not answered within 30 minutes (`ATLAS_JUDGE_WAIT_MIN`), the OpenAI judge decides, within 0.25 USD a day (`ATLAS_JUDGE_OPENAI_USD`); past that, stories keep waiting for Claude, and a story nobody judged in 48 hours is held. **Outcome.** Verified or partly verified items publish; anything else goes to `held.json` and never appears anywhere. Reported versus Confirmed: one source publishes as reported, naming the outlet; a second independent source or the primary document makes it confirmed.

jobs.style_guide:
## 1. The Standard

**Accurate first, then clear, then quick.** Every fact matches the source. Simplifying never changes a fact: a rounded
number that changes the meaning, a dropped "reportedly" or a claim the source does not make is an error, not style.

**No editorializing.** We report what happened and what the source says. We never add a verdict: no "notable",
"significant", "groundbreaking", "signals", "underscores", "paves the way", "crucial". If the source calls something
major, we credit that to the source. (code: an evaluative word the source never uses holds the story; judge)

**Facts can be funny; opinions are not news.** Wit lives in the emails' titles, opener and closing joke, never in a
claim (section 4).

## 2. Story Cards on the Site

A card is a headline and one line under it. A reader skimming the page should get the news from the headline alone and
the "so what" from the line.

**Headline: the news as a small story.** Subject, a strong concrete verb, and the result or a contrast. At most 12
words, sentence case. (code: length; writer; judge)
- Good: "Airbnb's tiny fine-tuned Gemma matches frontier APIs at about 1% of the cost"
- Good: "Grok's makers hit with three suits alleging pirated books in training"
- Bad: "Amodo says it ran government compute verification demo" (no result)
- Bad: "Salesforce: GRPO usually outperforms external-teacher distillation" (label and jargon)

**Clear, not awkward (owner, 2026-11-09).** Read the headline aloud: it must sound like a sentence a person would say to a colleague. A reader should never have to parse it twice.
- Active voice, the actor as the subject. Never "review proposed by X"; write "X proposes". (code: passive, holds)
- The company or person is the subject, never a document: no "Event page says", "The post notes", "in an Anthropic post", "per X", "according to X's rundown". (code: document_subject, document_credit, hold)
- One story per headline. Never join two news items with "as" or "while". (code: two_stories, holds)
- A concrete verb for what was found, built, decided or measured; not "explores", "demos", "urges study of". (code: vague_verb)
- No noun piles: never three or more modifiers before a noun ("single-policy humanlike grasps"). Unpack them. (writer; judge)
- No stacked credentials at the start ("Truthful AI director Owain Evans urges ..."). At most three words of credential. (writer; judge)
- A paper's own method, metric or product names stay out unless widely known; say what it does. (writer; judge)
- Full names, never a first name alone ("CEO Rahul"). (writer; judge)
- The line is a full sentence with its own subject, never "Recommends ...". (code: fragment, holds)
- Bad: "Subliminal learning, phantom transfer review proposed by Truthful AI director Owain Evans". Good: "Owain Evans calls for tests of hidden traits passing between models".
- Bad: "GenRobot to present human-data systems at CoRL Research Night" / "Event page says GenRobot will present ...". Good: "GenRobot will show its human-data capture systems at CoRL" / "The robot data vendor says the systems record people's movements to train embodied AI."
- Bad: "Hyundai and AIM explore NVIDIA's OpenShell as LG opens K-EXAONE-2.5 API". Good: one headline per story.

**Open with what happened, not who said it.** Credit once, naturally: a possessive ("in Airbnb's tests"), the maker as
the subject ("Moonshot AI released"), or a short ending ("Snorkel AI finds"). Never "X says" in both the headline and
the line. (code: credit_first, credit_twice; judge)

**The line adds what the headline leaves out.** The comparison, the scale, the catch, or who it affects, as the source
states it. It never restates the headline and never leans on it with "That is..." or "The aim is...". At most 24 words.
(code: repeats_headline holds the story, idea_length; judge)
- Headline: "Reflection AI cuts its model's needless refusals almost in half"
- Line: "Handshake, the career network behind Handshake AI, says it helped design the tests, and refusals of valid requests fell 3.1%."

**Few numbers, each with its meaning.** At most two key numbers across the headline and line; round to the meaning up
front ("almost in half") and keep the exact figure in the bullets. Never a number before what it measures; never
"percentage points" (write before and after). (code: too_many_numbers, percentage_points; judge)

**Plain words, field terms.** RL, SFT, eval, benchmark, rollout and LLM judge are fine. A paper's own acronyms, metric
names and method names are described in plain words or left out ("42% less compute", not "42.0% fewer total FLOPs").
(writer; judge)

**People get a short credential.** Two or three words from their verified role, before the name (or in the line when the headline would get long): "Illinois professor
Talia Ringer", "NVIDIA post-training lead Oleksii Kuchaiev". Never a credential the role does not state. (code:
person_label; judge)

**Lesser-known companies get a short descriptor** on first mention, 2 to 6 words, from their Directory line or what the
source says: "data vendor Julius AI". Never a guess: a company neither source nor Directory describes stays bare.
Well-known companies are named bare. (code: company_label; judge)

**Research papers say where the authors work.** Name the authors' companies or universities, as the paper's affiliation lines give them, in the headline, the first sentence or the summary's opening: "A Meta and NYU paper ...". Never an affiliation the paper does not show. (code: affiliation; writer; audit)

**Relay accounts are never the credit.** An account that only posts other people's papers or news (DailyPapers,
AK, digests) is not the maker; credit the authors or the organization. (code: relay_credit holds the story)

**Variety.** Headlines should not read like a template. Mix shapes: result first, a contrast ("but", "despite"), a
person with their credential, a number. (code: same_opening for generic openings; the headline editor sees the last
12 headlines; judge)

**Straight headlines on the site.** No puns or pop-culture jokes on the site: its headlines are read alone in search,
RSS and share previews. Vivid verbs give it life ("catches", "halves", "stops saying no").

**Legal stories** say "alleges", "sued over" or "reportedly" and name the outlet. Never a joke about a lawsuit, a
layoff or a named person's misfortune. (code: allegation words; writer)

## 3. Bullets

Each bullet is evidence for the line or one new fact: the numbers with their baseline, the method, who is involved, the
catch. None repeats the headline or the line. At most 22 words each. (writer; judge)

jobs.instructions:
A story is waiting to be published and you are its independent judge: a different model family from the writer and the fact checker. Nothing goes live until you answer, so answer judge jobs first and quickly. Judge the ITEM against the SOURCE TEXT ("text") only, never from memory or the web, exactly as these rules say:

You audit one published item of Atlas by Lorm against its SOURCE TEXT. You did not write the item. Judge from the SOURCE TEXT only, never from memory.

Part 1, evidence: for each reader-facing field (headline, idea, each bullet, summary, practice_takeaway) give the passage of the SOURCE TEXT that supports it, copied word for word: one sentence, or two adjacent sentences, up to 60 words, no ellipses, no paraphrase, exactly as it appears. A field may be supported by a passage already used for another field. If no passage supports the field, write "" and say so in Part 2. A practice_takeaway that only draws a direct consequence from a supported fact counts as supported by that fact's passage.

Part 2, critical errors, each pass or fail with a reason of at most 20 words:
- wrong_number: a number, unit, score or baseline differs from the source
- wrong_number_context: a number is right but its scope or comparison is not (e.g. 'beats X' when the source says 'on one subset')
- wrong_party: credit or blame given to the wrong company, lab, author or outlet
- self_report_as_fact: a company's claim about itself written as established fact, with no credit to the company anywhere in the headline or first sentence
- allegation_as_fact: an accusation, lawsuit claim or report stated as fact without 'alleges', 'reportedly', 'sues' or a court finding
- not_in_source: a claim the source text does not contain
- lost_qualifier: a qualifier dropped: preliminary, small test, proposed, reportedly, in one setting
- wrong_date_or_status: a proposal described as adopted, a preprint as peer-reviewed, a wrong date
- wrong_link: the item describes a different page than its link
- wrong_main_point: the headline is not what the source is mainly saying or announcing: a promotion, recap, roundup or list that mentions other news as examples, written up as that news; also when the item's source_kind or source_point does not describe the source correctly
- old_news_as_new: the source refers back to news announced earlier ('this week', 'last month', a list of recent raises) and the item presents it as new

Part 3, minor problems (list the codes that apply): over_limit, unclear, hype_or_filler, number_without_context, style.

Rules: a company's own numbers must be credited to it once, in the headline or the first sentence, in any natural form ("says", "reports", "according to", "in its tests", "its own benchmark", "the company claims"); credit given once is enough, and a headline without "says" passes when the first sentence carries the credit; allegations need "alleges", "reportedly", "sues" or a court finding; "percentage points" is a minor style problem, a wrong direction of change is wrong_number. Different wording for the same fact is NOT an error (an "env" is an RL environment; "raised $16M" and "a $16 million round" are the same claim): not_in_source fails only when the fact or claim itself is absent from the source, or the item asserts more than the source does. A number that appears in the source in another form (words, a table, a different unit that converts exactly) is in the source. A 2 to 6 word descriptor of a company drawn from the ATLAS DIRECTORY lines at the end of the SOURCE TEXT ("data vendor Julius AI"), or a short credential for the author that matches the item's who.role ("OpenAI researcher Hamel Husain"), is supported. If the SOURCE TEXT is clearly not the page the item describes, fail wrong_link. If the SOURCE TEXT is empty or unreadable, set every class to "unknown".

Return JSON:
{"evidence": {"headline": "quote", "idea": "quote", "bullets": ["quote per bullet"], "summary": "quote", "practice_takeaway": "quote or empty"},
 "critical": {"<class>": {"verdict": "pass" | "fail" | "unknown", "why": "..."}, ...},
 "minor": ["code", ...]}

Part 4, house style (only when the story passes Parts 1 to 3): read the job's "style_guide" and "style_failures". If the headline or idea breaks the guide (the listed failures, or anything else in it: a verdict the source does not make, jargon, a missing credential, the line restating the headline, a template-like shape), add "rewrite" with a new headline and idea that follow every rule. Use ONLY facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM (and company_note for a descriptor); keep every qualifier and the credit for a company's own claim. The server applies it only if it adds nothing new and passes the code checks. If the story already reads well, leave "rewrite" out.

Part 5, the headline (only when the job has "headline_rules"; the story passed Parts 1 to 3): you are also its headline editor, replacing a paid model (owner, 2026-11-10). Always add "rewrite" with a headline and idea written exactly as "headline_rules" says, varying the shape from "recent_headlines". The same limits apply: only facts, numbers and names already in the ITEM, written exactly as the ITEM writes them ("seven million" stays "seven million", not "7 million"), every qualifier kept, at most 12 words in the headline and 22 in the idea. If the ITEM's own headline and idea already follow every rule, send them back unchanged.
jobs.rubric:
## Gate 4: Write-Up and Fact Check

**Question.** Is every claim in the source, with nothing added and nothing lost?

**Write-up** (`DISTILL_SYSTEM`, strong model): one item in the shared schema (`seed/SCHEMA.md`), from the source text only, under the schema's "Every item makes its point" rule (the headline, first sentence and bullets each carry the finding). Plain language rules: full sentences, standard terms, numbers with context, headline at most 12 words, no hype words, no dashes, quotes under 15 words, absolute dates. A source with nothing of substance is skipped.

**Fact check** (`CHECK_SYSTEM`, strong model, a separate call that sees only the item and the source and is told it did not write it). Nine checks: source and date; every claim and bullet; the author's role and credibility; evidence type; plain language and limits; stated stakes; `control` and figures; quote-post attribution; allegations framed as allegations.

**Code checks after the model** (plan.md section 6.2, all free):

1. Every number in the item appears in the source (`numcheck`).
2. Every organization and person named appears in the source.
3. The date matches the source or its stated event date.
4. The link is the page that was read.
5. Lawsuit items carry alleges, accused, sued or reportedly in the headline and idea.
6. An item from the company's own site or account is marked a self-report.
7. Word limits, banned phrases, dashes.
11. Clear wording (owner, 2026-11-09, `atlas/style.py`, critical): no passive credit ("proposed by X"), no document as the subject ("Event page says", "The post notes"), no "per X" or "in X's post" in the headline, no first sentence without a subject, no two stories joined by "as" or "while". The headline editor gets these rules and retries once with the rule it broke; a story that still fails is held and repaired by the Claude agent. Noun piles, stacked credentials, paper-only names and first names alone are judge rules (docs/style.md, "Clear, not awkward").
8. The first sentence does not repeat the headline (`rubric.repeats`: 70% or more of the headline's words opening the first sentence fails; owner, 2026-11-08). The headline editor retries once; a story that still repeats is held and repaired by the Claude agent. The Daily's rows use the same check.
12. Full papers (owner, 2026-11-08): a story about an arXiv paper is written and checked from the full paper (arxiv.org/html, `net.page_text`), not the abstract page, which leaves out the authors' affiliations and table numbers and wrongly flagged 17 correct stories as partly verified. Claude audits, repairs and judge jobs get up to 120,000 characters of the paper (`claude_jobs.with_full_paper`); the OpenAI writer still sees `SOURCE_CHARS`. A paper story must name its authors' companies or universities (`style` check `affiliation`).
11. Pure shares (owner, 2026-11-08): an X post that only shares someone else's work, with no opinion or new information, is never the link or the credit. The writer marks it (`relay`, `original_url`); code moves the link to the original only when it is one of the post's or the poster's own replies' links (paper-listing pages map to arXiv), on a trusted site or the maker's own site (`trust.company_own`), and keeps the post as `shared_by` (`pipeline.share_original`). Government sites (.gov, gov.uk, .gc.ca, europa.eu and similar) are trusted.
10. House style (`atlas/style.py`, guide `docs/style.md`): editorializing (an evaluative word the source never uses) holds the story; headline and line length, credit first or twice, too many numbers, percentage points, a person without a credential, a lesser-known company without a descriptor and a generic repeated opening are listed for the Claude judge, whose rewrite is applied only when every number (small ones included) and name in it is already in the judged story and it passes these checks (`pipeline.apply_style_rewrite`). Since 2026-11-08 every number in a Claude fix, repair or rewrite must be in the source, including numbers of 10 and under (`pipeline.strict_numbers_missing`).
9. A relay account that only posts other people's paper links (DailyPapers @HuggingPapers, AK @_akhaliq) is never credited in the headline or first sentence (`rubric.RELAY_HANDLES`); the paper's authors or organization are.

**Error classes.** The audit and the gate use the two classes defined once in [plan.md section 6.1](plan.md#61-error-classes): a critical error (wrong number, wrong person, claim not in the source and the rest) fails the item outright; minor errors are allowed at most one per ten items.

**Rubric gate** (`atlas/rubric.py`, since 2026-11-05): after the fact check, a second model call that did not write or check the item applies the error classes of plan.md 6.1 one by one and must quote, word for word, the source sentence behind the headline, the first sentence, each bullet, the summary and the takeaway. Code verifies every quote is really in the source text (five words or more, exact after normalizing case and spacing) and runs the free checks (numbers, names, link, allegation words, self-report, limits). Any critical failure, or a headline or first sentence with no verified quote, holds the item. An unreadable source or an "unknown" class makes a verified item partly verified, with the reason shown. The verified quotes are stored on the item (`rubric.evidence`) so a later audit can re-check without a model. Switch: `ATLAS_RUBRIC_GATE=off`.

**Who judges (owner, 2026-11-08).** The owner's Claude agent, a different model family from the gpt-5-mini writer and checker, so the gate is an independent judge. A finished story waits in `parts/judge_wait.json`; the server starts the "Atlas judge" routine through its API trigger (`claude_jobs.fire_judge`, at most every 4 minutes, prompt in `tools/judge_routine_prompt.md`), and the agent answers a "judge" job in the same JSON shape as the OpenAI judge. Code verifies every quote and runs the same checks, then publishes or holds (`pipeline.judge_done`). If Claude has not answered within 30 minutes (`ATLAS_JUDGE_WAIT_MIN`), the OpenAI judge decides, within 0.25 USD a day (`ATLAS_JUDGE_OPENAI_USD`); past that, stories keep waiting for Claude, and a story nobody judged in 48 hours is held. Stories Claude judged are not audited again by Claude; stories the OpenAI judge decided still get the Claude audit. Until `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_URL` and `ATLAS_JUDGE_FIRE_TOKEN` are set, or with `ATLAS_JUDGE=openai`, the OpenAI judge runs on every story as before.

**Outcome.** Verified or partly verified items publish; anything else goes to `held.json` and never appears anywhere. Reported versus Confirmed: one source publishes as reported, naming the outlet; a second independent source or the primary document makes it confirmed.
